extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of international law; legal historians; counsel dealing with maritime prize and law-of-war issues
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of legal standards and procedural rules governing conduct in war (limits of violence, immunities, property rights) and the law of prizes/privateering, including prize-court procedure and appellate practice. Intended as a practical-legal summary rather than pure theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity as measure of violence in war
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessity is the measure of violence in war, and humanity its tempering spirit; the rights of war are to be measured by the objects of the war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lawfulness of the end only permits the bare means necessary to attain it; actions beyond necessary means are condemned by natural law and conscience. What is just in one situation may be wrongful in another; right goes hand in hand with necessity and the exigency of the case. Killing enemies is only lawful when gentler methods are insufficient to compel submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons generally exempt from direct military operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain classes are generally considered exempt from the operations of war, unless actually taking up arms or committing misconduct to forfeit immunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted Wheaton: the sovereign and his family, members of the civil government, women and children, cultivators of the earth, artisans, labourers, merchants, men of science and letters, and generally all persons engaged in ordinary civil pursuits are exempt unless actually taken in arms or guilty of misuse violating the usages of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private property on land generally exempt from confiscation
rubrics_metrics.description: Private property on land is exempt from confiscation, except where it becomes booty in special cases (taken from enemies in the field or besieged towns) or in military contributions levied upon inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemption extends even to absolute conquest; private property is not usually taken without compensation. Historical practices of total confiscation are exceptional; contributions may be levied in lieu of confiscation for necessities or expenses of occupation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government (public) property vests in victor
rubrics_metrics.description: Property belonging to the government of the vanquished passes to the victorious state, which takes the place of the former sovereign with respect to eminent domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes public/state property (transferable on conquest) from private property protected by exemptions and compensation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to make war belongs to the sovereign; subjects require orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the sovereign power has the right to make war; subjects are not allowed to commit hostile acts without orders from their sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign orders may be general (declaration of war) or particular (commissions to generals, officers, privateersmen, partisans). A general declaration authorises subjects to secure persons and things of the enemy when they fall into their hands, but does not invite offensive expeditions without commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privateering requires sovereign commission (letters of marque)
rubrics_metrics.description: Private armed vessels require commissions or letters of marque from the sovereign to lawfully act as privateers; fitting out vessels without licence was forbidden from the 15th century onward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noncommissioned captors in war may capture hostile ships without being deemed pirates, but they have no interest in prizes (property condemned to the government) and rewards are discretionary with the Admiralty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-commissioned captors' rights and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Hostilities without commission are contrary to usage and irregular but not treated as piracy during war; such captors' seizures are condemned to the government as 'Droits of the Admiralty'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners of noncommissioned captures have no proprietary interest; reward is left to Admiralty liberality and often adjudicated by Admiralty Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruits of forcible detention before hostilities belong to the Crown
rubrics_metrics.description: The fruits of forcible detention or occupancy prior to hostilities vest in the crown; similarly, domestic property taken in contravention of trade laws is condemned to the Crown, not individual captors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customary exceptions (e.g., customs/excise vessels commissioned with letters of marque) reserve interest to the Crown to deter diversion from duties to privateering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants to Admiralty and limits of Crown rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The Crown's original rights of prize may be granted in whole or part to the Lord High Admiral; such a grant alienates Crown rights unless restored by Parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes Admiralty rights: vessels coming into ports by distress or ignorance of war may belong to the Admiral; where violence connected with war has been exercised, rights belong to the Crown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privateers' acquisition of captures is by sovereign grant and conditioned by contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons fitting out private vessels under commission acquire property of captures as compensation, but only by grant from the sovereign; the sovereign may allow whole or part shares per the contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privateers are required by commercial ordinances to give adequate security to conduct cruises according to laws and usages of war, respect rights of neutrals, and bring prizes in for adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privateer commissions do not extend to private property on land
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissions of privateers do not include capture of private property upon land; Prize Act language limits captors to certain land objects when captured by Her Majesty's ships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privateers were intentionally restricted to water-borne property and fortified places to prevent depredations against individuals on enemy coasts and to avoid incentives for unauthorised land raids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on sharing prizes when sailing in company or under convoy
rubrics_metrics.description: A privateer sailing under convoy of a Queen's ship takes no share in prizes taken by the convoying royal ship unless ordered to give chase or actually aiding; when sailing in company, shares depend on actual contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sir William Scott: 'takers' naturally include those who actually take possession or render actual endeavour; mere common enterprise is insufficient — there must be some actual contribution of endeavour at commencement or during engagement or preparations for chase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive captor criterion (entitlement to prize share)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be entitled as a captor (including constructive captors), a vessel must have actually contributed endeavour or rendered constructive assistance — mere presence or prior association is not enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being in sight a day or two before is insufficient; entitlement arises if in sight at commencement, in the act of chasing, preparing for chase, or afterwards during its continuance; there must be specific contribution beyond general intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privateers v. Pirates — definitional and behavioral standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A privateer differs from a pirate in having a sovereign commission, operating under a state of war (or reprisals), and being obliged to observe instructions; a pirate plunders indiscriminately in peace or war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privateers may become pirates if they transgress the limits prescribed to them. Privateers must attack only enemy ships or neutral vessels engaged in illicit commerce and follow the laws of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on subjects accepting foreign letters of marque without permission
rubrics_metrics.description: States generally prohibit their subjects from accepting letters of marque from foreign powers without sovereign permission; many treaties impose such prohibitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutral subjects taking foreign commissions may not be punished as pirates if they have letters patent from a belligerent, though their ships may be confiscated. Domestic laws (e.g., U.S.) forbid citizens from assisting private vessels to cruise against friendly powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title to property taken in war vests in captor after possession (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Title to property taken in war is generally divested from the original owner and transferred to the captor upon the captor's firm possession; for personal property, possession is commonly regarded as firm after twenty-four hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ships and goods captured at sea are excepted from some local rules. Primary right to captures rests in the sovereign; individuals have interest only by grant from the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prizes must be brought into port and adjudicated by competent prize court
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prize is taken at sea, it must be brought into port with due care for adjudication by a competent prize court of the captor's government; condemnation must be pronounced by that court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prize court should be of the captor's nation (a prize court of an ally cannot condemn). The prize is appraised and proceedings follow statutory and admiralty forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures preliminary to condemnation (papers, examinations, monition, claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon bringing a prize into port, the captor delivers upon oath all papers found; preparatory examinations of captain and crew are taken; a written monition is extracted and served notifying capture and calling interested parties to appear within twenty days, after which causes are heard if claims exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutral masters typically make a protest and forward instructions; claimants file claims supported by affidavit and must provide security (e.g., sixty pounds) to answer costs if claim fraudulent. If captor neglects, claimants may compel production of papers and proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate practice and security on appeal (inhibition, time limits, security amounts)
rubrics_metrics.description: If dissatisfied with sentence, a proctor must enter an appeal (within fourteen days) and apply for an inhibition instrument (within three months for High Court sentences, nine months for Vice-Admiralty), giving security (commonly two hundred pounds) to answer costs if the appeal is vexatious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inhibition suspends further proceedings in the inferior court and directs transmission of proceedings to the superior tribunal; service may be effected by various methods including affixing to residence if person cannot be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of proof and plea-and-proof procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of proof required depends on the degree of suspicion or doubt; in cases of heavy suspicion, the court may order 'plea and proof', allowing regular pleadings and witness examination instead of relying only on affidavits and documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further proof may include affidavits by asserted proprietors, original correspondence, bills of lading, invoices, extracts from books, all authenticated and sworn before competent magistrates or British Consul; standing commissions may be sent abroad to receive witness examinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize Court jurisdiction and objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction over prizes is exercised by the Admiralty judge (Prize Court) and is distinct from other courts; the purpose is to suspend property pending condemnation, punish captors' misbehaviour, restore property if groundless, and finally condemn lawful prize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A captor may force all interested parties to defend; common-law courts are not always excluded for non-prize seizures; the nature of the question, not locality, determines jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on where prize courts can act; conclusiveness of judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: A prize court of the capturing nation has exclusive authority to determine prize; it cannot lawfully act in neutral territory and a prize court of an ally cannot condemn. Judgments of prize courts are conclusive on property questions within the captor's nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a sentence is manifestly unjust or contrary to the Law of Nations, the state (not captors) is responsible and unjust sentences can justify reprisals. Practice has sometimes stretched principles (e.g., condemning prizes in England lying in neutral ports), but correct principle restricts jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of immoveable property taken in war (conquest v. treaty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Immoveable possessions (lands, towns, provinces) become the property of the conqueror only by treaty of peace or by complete subjugation/extinction of the state; until such confirmation, acquisition is incomplete and liable to jus postliminii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purchasers of conquered land take at peril of eviction by original sovereign until sovereignty is renounced or the property is confirmed by treaty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passports and safe-conducts as sovereign privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Passports and safe-conducts are sovereign privileges ensuring safety to persons or things in transit; they emanate from sovereign authority and are delegated to inferior officers, and the named person cannot transfer the privilege to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are a form of executive privilege or commission for safe passage and conveyance, and function as licences or permissions under sovereign authority.
